ukmt-jk-2022-01.title: Look at the neighbours
ukmt-jk-2022-01.body:
The hidden die touches the die above it (marked R) and the two bottom-level dice next to it (marked P and S). So its letter is not R, P or S. It must be Q.

**Answer: (B) Q**

ukmt-jk-2022-02.title: Time difference
ukmt-jk-2022-02.body:
When it is $8$ am in San Francisco it is $5$ pm in Madrid, so Madrid is $9$ hours ahead. $9$ pm yesterday plus $9$ hours is $6$ am today.

**Answer: (E) 6 am today**

ukmt-jk-2022-03.title: Work from the end
ukmt-jk-2022-03.body:
They ate $1+3+3+2=9$ pieces, leaving $16$, which is $8$ apples and $8$ pears. Pears eaten: $3+2=5$. So the original number of pears was $8+5=13$.

**Answer: (B) 13**

ukmt-jk-2022-04.title: Compare
ukmt-jk-2022-04.body:
Adding a second balloon increases the load capacity by $180-80=100$ kg, so one balloon lifts $100$ kg in total (basket plus contents). With contents $80$ kg, the basket weighs $100-80=20$ kg.

**Answer: (B) 20**

ukmt-jk-2022-04.title: Equations
ukmt-jk-2022-04.body:
Let a balloon lift $L$ and the basket weigh $b$: $L-b=80$ and $2L-b=180$. Subtract: $L=100$, so $b=20$.

**Answer: (B) 20**

ukmt-jk-2022-05.title: Remainders mod 4
ukmt-jk-2022-05.body:
Yellow numbers leave remainder $3$ on division by $4$, blue numbers leave remainder $2$. Their sum leaves remainder $5\equiv1$, which is red. So the answer is always red.

**Answer: (E) only red**

ukmt-jk-2022-06.title: Count roads
ukmt-jk-2022-06.body:
Five cities, each joined to the other four: $5\times4/2=10$ roads in all. Alice's map shows $7$. Missing: $10-7=3$.

**Answer: (D) 3**

ukmt-jk-2022-08.title: Compare the straight edges
ukmt-jk-2022-08.body:
Both perimeters contain the arcs of the four quarter circles. The first shape also has straight edges of $10,10,5,5$ cm in its boundary, while the second has only one straight edge of $10$ cm. Difference: $10+10+5+5-10=20$ cm.

**Answer: (D) 20**

ukmt-jk-2022-09.title: Place them
ukmt-jk-2022-09.body:
Guy sits between Fay and Ian, so Fay, Guy, Ian are consecutive. The remaining two seats go to Huw and Jen. Jen is not next to Ian, so Jen is next to Fay and Huw sits next to Ian.

**Answer: (A) Fay and Huw**

ukmt-jk-2022-11.title: Chase angles
ukmt-jk-2022-11.body:
$\angle PTQ=180-154=26^\circ$ (straight line $PTS$). Since $PQ=QT$, triangle $PQT$ is isosceles with $\angle TPQ=26^\circ$, so $\angle TQP=180-52=128^\circ$. As $QT\parallel RS$, corresponding angles give $\angle SRQ=128^\circ$.

**Answer: (E) 128**

ukmt-jk-2022-12.title: Track the heights
ukmt-jk-2022-12.body:
The window covers heights $5$ m to $6$ m. First the ball falls from $10$ m past the window: $1$ appearance. It rebounds to $8$ m, above the window, so it passes the window going up and again going down: $2$ more ($3$). It rebounds to $6.4$ m, again above the window: $2$ more ($5$). It rebounds to $5.12$ m, which enters the bottom of the window and then falls back out the same way: $1$ more ($6$). The next rebound is $4.096$ m, below the window. Total $6$.

**Answer: (D) 6**

ukmt-jk-2022-13.title: Angles at the centre
ukmt-jk-2022-13.body:
Folding in half three times gives a triangle whose angle at the centre is $\frac12\cdot\frac12\cdot\frac12\cdot360^\circ=45^\circ$. The cut is at $90^\circ$ to a side, so the cut-off corner has angles $45^\circ$ and $45^\circ$ at the base, and the unfolded hole has corner angles $2\times45^\circ=90^\circ$. By symmetry, the hole is a square with a horizontal top side, as in C.

**Answer: (C)**

ukmt-jk-2022-14.title: Fill in the counts
ukmt-jk-2022-14.body:
Four guests aged $6$, and $8$ is the most common age so at least five are $8$. There are $8$ other guests, and each of $7,9,10$ appears at least once. With five $8$s that leaves $3$ guests: exactly one each of $7,9,10$. Total age: $24+5\cdot8+7+9+10=90$, mean $90/12=7.5$.

**Answer: (D) 7.5**

ukmt-jk-2022-15.title: Side length
ukmt-jk-2022-15.body:
With side $x$: $V=x^3$ and surface area $6x^2=2x^3$, so $x=3$ and $V=27$.

**Answer: (C) 27**

ukmt-jk-2022-16.title: Count the circle
ukmt-jk-2022-16.body:
If $n$ children are between them one way, $6n$ the other way. Including Anna and Zara the class has $7n+2$ children. The only number between $20$ and $30$ of this form is $23$ ($n=3$).

**Answer: (A) 23**

ukmt-jk-2022-17.title: Opposite rectangles
ukmt-jk-2022-17.body:
If a rectangle is cut by one horizontal and one vertical line, the perimeters of two diagonally opposite small rectangles add up to the perimeter of $WXYZ$ (together they use two full widths and two full heights). So the four perimeters split into two pairs with equal sums. If the smallest and largest were in different pairs, say $m+x=M+y$, then $x-y=M-m$, forcing $x=M$ and $y=m$, impossible. So the smallest and largest are diagonally opposite. The unknown perimeter lies between $11$ and $19$, so the smallest and largest are $11$ and $19$, and the perimeter of $WXYZ$ is $11+19=30$.

**Answer: (B) 30**

ukmt-jk-2022-18.title: Find the gap
ukmt-jk-2022-18.body:
$3+5\times7-9=29$, which is $7$ short of $36$. Increasing the $5$ by $1$ adds $7$ (one more $7$). So $5$.

**Answer: (B) 5**

ukmt-jk-2022-19.title: Start from 12
ukmt-jk-2022-19.body:
The only numbers within $2$ of $12$ are $10$ and $11$, so they sit on either side of $12$. Next to $11$ the only unused number within $2$ is $9$; next to $10$ it is $8$. So $10$ is adjacent to $8$ in the circle, and the arrangement continues uniquely as $8,10,12,11,9,\dots$. In the completed circle the only odd-even neighbours are $11$-$12$ and $1$-$2$, so options A to D (which each pair an odd and an even number) are impossible, while $8$ and $10$ are adjacent.

**Answer: (E) 8 and 10**

ukmt-jk-2022-20.title: Try the largest square
ukmt-jk-2022-20.body:
A $6\times6$ square leaves a $6\times1$ strip, giving $7$ squares in total. A $5\times5$ square leaves a $5\times1$ strip (five unit squares) plus a $6\times2$ part needing at least three more, so more than $7$. A $4\times4$ square can be placed with two $2\times2$ squares (filling the $4\times2$ strip beside it) and two $3\times3$ squares (filling the remaining $3\times6$ block): $5$ squares. Fewer than $5$ is impossible: if the largest square is at most $3\times3$, then $4$ squares cover at most $36<42$; and larger squares were checked above to give $5$ or more.

**Answer: (B) 5**

ukmt-jk-2022-21.title: Check each table
ukmt-jk-2022-21.body:
The row totals and the column totals must both equal the number of painted cells. A: the top row has $4$ painted cells but a column has $0$: impossible. B: row sum $7$, column sum $8$: impossible. C: the bottom two rows have no painted cells but a column needs $3$: impossible. E: the top row has none but the second and fourth columns each have $3$ painted cells and the bottom row has only $1$: impossible. So D, for which an arrangement exists.

**Answer: (D)**

ukmt-jk-2022-22.title: Add the five lines
ukmt-jk-2022-22.body:
Let the top number be $p$ and each line sum $X$. The five lines cover $p$ three times and every other circle twice, so $5X=p+2(1+2+\dots+7)=p+56$. So $p+56$ is a multiple of $5$, which among $1$ to $7$ forces $p=4$ (then $X=12$). An example exists: top $4$, then $3,7,2$ for the next row and $5,1,6$ below.

**Answer: (C) 4**

ukmt-jk-2022-23.title: Divide into 16 squares
ukmt-jk-2022-23.body:
Divide the square into $16$ congruent small squares, each of area $64/16=4$ cm$^2$. After the two folds each shaded rectangle is made up of two small squares, so the total shaded area is $2\times2\times4=16$ cm$^2$.

**Answer: (D) 16 cm$^2$**

ukmt-jk-2022-24.title: Place values
ukmt-jk-2022-24.body:
The sum is $100p+10q+r+10q+r+r=100p+20q+3r=912$. So $3r$ ends in $2$, giving $r=4$. Then $100p+20q=900$, i.e. $5p+q=45$; with $q$ a nonzero digit $q=5$, $p=8$ (number $854+54+4=912$).

**Answer: (C) 5**

ukmt-jk-2022-25.title: Follow the statements
ukmt-jk-2022-25.body:
If Ria had $1$ she would know Sylvie's number is $2$. So Ria's number is not $1$, and Sylvie (hearing this) knows that. If Sylvie had $1$, she would know Ria's is $2$. Sylvie did not say she knew, so Sylvie's number is not $1$ and Ria learns that. If Sylvie had $2$ she would now know Ria has $3$ (since Ria is not $1$), so she would have known; she didn't, so Sylvie does not have $2$. Ria now knows: if Ria has $2$, Sylvie has $1$ or $3$, but Sylvie is not $1$, so $3$; if Ria has $3$, Sylvie has $2$ or $4$, but not $2$, so $4$. For $4$ or more Ria could not be sure. Of the options only $2$ works.

**Answer: (B) 2**
